problem_type: loopback fixture keep-alive expiry races a later batch submission
symptom: The full unit suite intermittently fails agentPanelSpendBatches S06 after about 49 seconds: shot-33 ends submission_unknown with SubmissionReceiptUnknownError: fetch failed instead of all 33 loopback submissions becoming ready.
direct_cause: The shared spend-confirm loopback server advertises Node's default five-second keep-alive window. Under full-suite event-loop stalls, Undici reused one of two pooled sockets 6.121 seconds after its previous response, just after the server's five-second timeout plus one-second keepAliveTimeoutBuffer destroyed it. Request 33 emitted bodySent and then ECONNRESET in one millisecond, but the server never emitted server-request for it.
class_root: A deterministic HTTP vendor fixture allowed persistent client sockets even though connection reuse is outside the fixture contract, making test outcomes depend on the race between the server's idle-socket timer and the client's processing of that close.
affected_population: The 33-shot S06 spend-confirm batch under full-suite CPU and event-loop load
Every spend-confirm test using the shared startLoopbackVendor fixture when a pooled connection is idle near the Node server timeout
internal_only_reason: The invariant is the repository's own fixture contract: submissions must exercise HTTP request/response behavior without testing pooled connection reuse. Runtime introspection on the failing Node 22.22.0 process recorded keepAliveTimeout=5000 and keepAliveTimeoutBuffer=1000; the captured Undici/server diagnostic establishes the exact timing without requiring an external behavioral assumption.
invariants: Every response from the shared spend-confirm loopback vendor makes that connection ineligible for a later submission.
A transport failure whose receipt is uncertain remains submission_unknown; the fixture repair does not retry or reclassify it.
All spend-confirm callers using startLoopbackVendor receive the same connection lifecycle policy.

door_reduction.why_not: The generated map includes two true shared-helper consumers plus independent, file-local helpers with the same unqualified symbols. Those local fixtures belong to separate test journeys and do not converge on the spend-confirm helper; consolidating them would expand this transport-lifecycle repair. The shared spend-confirm server remains the single enforcement door for both affected consumers.

generality_proof: The response policy is enforced by startLoopbackVendor before any shared spend-confirm caller receives its origin. Both the long batch suite and the individual confirmation suite therefore use non-reusable response connections, so no submission can inherit an idle socket owned by this fixture. Independent same-named fixtures were inspected separately and do not call this boundary.

shared_boundaries.responsibility: Own the HTTP server and response connection lifecycle for every shared spend-confirm vendor fixture.

same_class_entry_points.evidence: Imports the shared startLoopbackVendor; the captured failure occurred after 32 responses on that origin, and the changed regression proves its responses no longer leave a reusable socket.
Imports the same startLoopbackVendor for all of its loopback HTTP submissions and therefore inherits the response connection policy.
Defines a separate local server and provider rather than importing the spend-confirm helper; the diagnostic origin and failing test do not traverse it.
Defines an independent fixture with its own transport lifecycle; no failure from its origins appeared in the captured full-suite diagnostic.

recurrence.reason: The race depends on machine load and idle timing, so another full-suite run or another shared-helper caller can hit the same closed pooled socket even when focused runs pass.
same_class_scan: Ran node scripts/door-map.mjs --write=startLoopbackVendor,loopbackProvider --include-tests; it found both shared-helper consumers and four suites with independent same-named local helpers.
Inspected agentPanelSpendConfirm.e2e.test.ts and agentPanelSpendBatches.e2e.test.ts imports to confirm they converge on agentPanelSpendConfirmTestUtils.ts.

Inspected mcpMultiShotAnchorReuse.e2e.test.ts, mcpMultiShotCreateEntrance.e2e.test.ts, anchorCheckpointApproval.e2e.test.ts, and multiShotBatchScheduler.e2e.test.ts to confirm their helpers are file-local and outside the failing origin.

prevention.invariant: Shared spend-confirm loopback responses explicitly close their HTTP connection, so clients cannot pool a socket until the server's idle timer expires it.
prevention.failure_mode: A client that ignores the close contract receives a closed connection; the fixture never silently retries a submission or converts an uncertain receipt to ready.
prevention.strategy: Declare Connection: close at the fixture server's response boundary, which removes idle socket ownership from the fixture without changing hardenedFetch, the provider adapter, or submission classification.

legacy_paths.rationale: The shared helper remains the supported spend-confirm fixture. Its response lifecycle is made explicit in place; no alternate server or fallback path is introduced.

dependency_lifecycle.rationale: Node and Undici exposed the fixture's unspecified connection lifecycle, but the repair neither depends on nor works around a particular dependency release. HTTP Connection: close is the fixture-owned contract across supported runtime versions, so no dependency upgrade or retained fork is involved.

migration: No persisted state or production caller changes. Existing spend-confirm tests receive the explicit response policy the next time they start the shared loopback server.
residual_risks: Independent file-local loopback fixtures still use their own connection policies and would require separate evidence if they exhibit the same failure.
The root agent owns the later full desktop/unit validation; this repair is verified only with affected unit slices here.
